items.title: Somatic Symptom vs Factitious vs Malingering
items.content: **Do not infer intent from unexplained symptoms:** Somatic symptom disorder concerns disproportionate, persistent thoughts, feelings, or behavior around distressing physical symptoms; symptoms may accompany a medical condition and are not intentionally produced. Malingering is intentional symptom production for an identifiable external incentive and is not a mental disorder. items.title: OCD Diagnostic Features
items.content: **OCD recognition:** Obsessions are recurrent intrusive and unwanted thoughts, urges, or images; compulsions are repetitive behaviors or mental acts performed under a felt rule or in response to distress. items.title: Test Bias & Fairness
items.content: **Fairness concerns the validity of an intended interpretation and use:** Construct-irrelevant barriers can arise from language, disability access, administration, opportunity, familiarity, speed, or context; construct underrepresentation can omit important parts of what should be measured. Differential item functioning flags items with different response probabilities after matching on the measured attribute, but DIF is evidence to investigate, not automatic proof of bias. Prediction bias requires appropriate regression and criterion evidence, not different group means. Representative norms, translation and adaptation evidence, accessibility, standardized conditions, multiple methods, uncertainty, and consequences all matter. A "culture-fair" label or nonverbal format does not remove culture, and reliability alone does not establish validity or fairness.

items.title: Nonparametric Tests
items.content: **Procedure-specific assumptions remain:** Mann-Whitney, Wilcoxon signed-rank, Kruskal-Wallis, Friedman, Spearman, permutation, and exact tests answer different questions. items.title: Correlation Pitfalls
items.content: **Inspect before interpreting r:** Pearson correlation targets linear association and can be changed by outliers, nonlinearity, range restriction, mixtures, measurement error, and dependence. A strong coefficient can coexist with poor transport or confounding; a weak coefficient can conceal subgroup or curved relations. Squaring r has a specific linear-model interpretation, not a universal percent-causal explanation. Plot data, report uncertainty, and distinguish association from direction and causation.

items.title: Chi-Square Test
items.content: **Categorical-count tests:** Goodness-of-fit compares observed counts with a specified distribution; independence or homogeneity tests compare categorical distributions across variables or groups. items.title: Threats to Internal Validity
items.content: **Causal alternatives:** History, maturation, testing, instrumentation, selection, attrition, regression, contamination, and interactions can offer rival explanations for change. Random assignment and a concurrent control strengthen causal inference but do not automatically eliminate nonadherence, differential attrition, measurement problems, interference, or analysis bias. Diagnose threats from the actual assignment, timing, measurement, missingness, implementation, and estimand rather than treating "THIS MAID" as a universal checklist solution.

items.title: Type I vs Type II Errors
items.content: **Decision-error cue:** Type I error rejects a true null under a specified procedure; Type II error fails to reject a false null; power is the probability of rejection under a specified alternative. Alpha does not equal the probability that a reported finding is false, and one minus alpha is not power. Effect size, sample size, variability, design, multiplicity, assumptions, prior evidence, and consequences all shape interpretation.

items.content: **Competence is task and context specific:** Education, training, supervised experience, consultation, study, and appropriate experience support competence; new populations, technologies, languages, disabilities, emergencies, and legal roles may require additional preparation.
